item.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted, Electrocardiogram-Derived, Sequential Rule-Based Decision Tree for Exclusion of Acute Coronary Syndrome as the Etiology of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: After out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), deciding which patients without ST-segment elevation warrant emergency coronary angiography is difficult, as standard electrocardiogram (ECG), troponin, and echocardiography are limited in the early post-arrest window. We aimed to develop a sequential rule-based decision tree to identify post-ROSC patients in whom acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is unlikely to be the arrest etiology.

Methods: In this single-center retrospective study, adult patients with OHCA were divided into development (2020-2024; n=329) and temporal validation (2025; n=71) cohorts. Post-ROSC 12-lead ECGs were analyzed by a deep-learning platform generating ten digital biomarkers. Five candidate biomarkers were combined into a rhythm-stratified sequential decision tree under a zero false-negative constraint; its performance was compared with that of individual biomarkers and validated in the temporal cohort.

Results: The tree classified 171/329 (52.0%) and 32/71 (45.1%) patients in the development and validation cohorts, respectively, as "ACS not likely," with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified at any node. Yield concentrated in the non-shockable subgroup, in which the model excluded 169/261 (64.8%) non-ACS cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC], 0.824), outperforming each individual biomarker. In the shockable subgroup, which carries a high pretest probability of ACS, 38/40 patients (95.0%) were retained as "ACS not excluded."

Conclusions: A rhythm-stratified, rule-based decision tree combining AI-assisted ECG-derived biomarkers classified approximately half of post-OHCA patients as "ACS not likely" with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified, principally in the non-shockable subgroup. This transparent, bedside-deployable framework warrants prospective multicenter evaluation.

Choi A, Yoon H, Won Lee SG, Park C, Han E, Roh YH

item.title: Ventilation Monitoring in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Care
item.description:
Introduction: Adherence to American Heart Association (AHA) ventilation guidelines during cardiac arrest is challenging.

Methods: Prospective, Before/After quality assurance study determining adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by Milwaukee County Emergency Medical Services and Kenosha Fire in Wisconsin using (Before) end tidal carbon dioxide [ETCO2] to monitor ventilations - Real BVM Help® applied but blinded versus (After) Real BVM Help®.

Primary endpoints: mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in-target for rate, tidal volume, and both rate and tidal volume. AHA 2020 guidelines were followed.

Results: From 9/29/22-12/22/23, 278 patients were entered (148 Before/130 After). Average age: 62.3±16.7 years; 185 (67%) male. Mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in Before/After Groups in-target for rate (47.7±25.1% vs 74.4±24.1% respectively, p<0.0001), tidal volume (15.3±15.4% vs 45.4±23.8% respectively, p<0.0001), and rate and tidal volume (7.5±9.6% vs 39.0±23.3% respectively, p<0.0001) were significantly higher in the After Group. In the Before Group, using ETCO2 to monitor all ventilations (N=22,037 ventilations), only 43.8% were in-target for rate, 13.5% in-target for tidal volume, and 6.8% in-target for rate and tidal volume with a lower-than-target tidal volume delivered in 58.2% of all ventilations.

Conclusion: Real BVM Help® was associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines. ETCO2 monitoring failed to approach both rate and tidal volume guideline adherence with a lower-than-target tidal volume being the most common parameter delivered out-of-target (58.2%). Ventilation rate and tidal volume monitoring with real-time feedback should be considered during treatment of cardiac arrest.

Aufderheide TP, Colella MR, Weston BW, Labinski J, Mattrisch L, Jasti J

item.title: Early Identification of Recurrent Out-of-hospital Cardiac Arrest Using Clinical ECG Features
item.description:
Background: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) after initial return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is associated with relatively poor outcomes. Early identification of rearrest might allow for intervention to prevent rearrest. In this study, we sought to determine whether clinical ECG features can predict rearrest.

Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients who achieved ROSC between 2018-2024. We evaluated the association of ECG features (QRS width, standard deviation of NN intervals, root mean square of successive NN interval differences, and percentage of NN intervals that differ by more than 50 milliseconds) within individual 15-second segments throughout a 5-minute window prior to rearrest as well as their temporal trends over the 5-minute analytic window.

Results: Of the 1,489 OHCA patients achieving ROSC, 1,298 were analyzed; 528 (40.7%) experienced rearrest. Rearrest patients were older, less likely to receive bystander CPR (48.7% vs. 61.9%), and had lower survival (20.4% vs. 43.1%) and favorable neurologic outcomes (7.8% vs. 21.2%; all p<0.001). We found lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher HR variability in those with rearrest. Identification was highest 1 minute prior to rearrest (AUROC 0.74), declining beyond 3 minutes. Models using temporal trends achieved AUROC 0.67; strongest predictors were heart rate variability measures and QRS width.

Conclusion: Established ECG features achieved good prediction for rearrest with identification improving closer to time of rearrest. Future work leveraging novel features or more advanced artificial intelligence models may further improve prediction.

To D, Coult J, Mohamed I, Bhandari S, Sayre M, Kusztos A

Traumatic Emergency Thoracotomy for Resuscitation in Shock (TETRiS): a national service evaluation of resuscitative thoracotomy practice outside the operating theatre
item.description:
Background: Resuscitative thoracotomy (RT) is performed in patients with traumatic cardiac arrest or peri-arrest to treat potentially reversible causes of circulatory collapse. Optimal patient selection and timing remain uncertain, and existing evidence is largely retrospective, often excluding prehospital deaths. This prospective service evaluation examined contemporary RT practice and outcomes across a national major trauma system, including prehospital and emergency department settings.

Methods: Prospective 12-month observational study across 20 UK Helicopter Emergency Medical Services and 26 Major Trauma Centre Emergency Departments, using the PHOTON, TERN, and NaTRIC research networks.

Results: A total of 116 patients underwent RT, of which 82 (70.7%) were performed prehospital. Median age was 30 years, 97 patients (83.6%) were male, and 81 (69.8%) sustained penetrating injury. Suspected cardiac tamponade was the most common indication for RT (72/116 [62.1%]), although operative findings demonstrated exsanguinating haemorrhage in 82 patients (70.7%). Overall, 50 patients (43.1%) achieved return of spontaneous circulation and eight (6.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Survival was strongly associated with pathophysiological cause, duration of arrest, and physiological state at the time of intervention, with substantially better outcomes observed in patients with cardiac tamponade than exsanguination. Patients undergoing emergency department RT demonstrated shorter arrest durations, more favourable physiology, and higher survival than those undergoing prehospital RT. There were no survivors beyond 10 minutes of traumatic cardiac arrest.

Conclusion: In this prospective national evaluation of RT practice, outcomes were strongly associated with the pathophysiological cause and duration of arrest, and the residual physiology present at the time of intervention. The most favourable outcomes were observed in patients with cardiac tamponade and those undergoing RT before irreversible physiological deterioration.

Ramage L, Tucker H, Marsden ME, Wohlgemut JM, Naeem S, Christian M
